# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

## Rethinking What a Successful Meeting Looks Like

There is a common assumption, woven deep into workplace culture, that a good meeting is one where everyone walks out nodding. We celebrate alignment. We praise teams that "get on the same page." Managers often judge their own effectiveness by how smoothly discussions proceed and how rarely open conflict surfaces. Agreement feels like progress. Disagreement feels like friction, delay, dysfunction.

But this assumption deserves scrutiny, because agreement can be deceptive. People nod along for many reasons that have nothing to do with genuine conviction: they haven't had time to form an opinion, they're intimidated by a senior colleague, they're tired, they want the meeting to end, or they simply assume someone else has done the thinking. When a room full of people appears to agree, what you may actually have is a room full of people who haven't yet discovered what they disagree about. And undiscovered disagreement doesn't disappear. It resurfaces later—in half-hearted execution, in quiet sabotage, in the meeting after the meeting where the real opinions finally come out.
